Never-Ending Residential Cruise Villa Vie Odyssey Ceases Operations, Kicks Guests Off in Cambodia
19 photos
Photo: Villa Vie Residences (Composite)
They said it wouldn't last, and they were right. The "never-ending residential cruise" Villa Vie Odyssey, which company Villa Vie Residences promised would offer a new model of global living at sea, has has ended. Not with a whimper, but with a bang.
On October 27, Villa Vie Residences (VVR), a Florida-based startup with management ties to another residential cruise that was canceled in 2023 just days before it was supposed to take off, announced they had ceased operations. The Odyssey, the first of a planned series of three cruise ships, would go into dock in Cambodia indefinitely, while management tried to find new financing.
When the announcement came, the Odyssey had been sailing almost non-stop for two whole years, after a departure that itself became a sort of odyssey after repeated delays. The ship carried 203 guests and 156 crew, with all the guests and a big chunk of the crew, disembarked in a cargo port in Cambodia almost forcefully.
The Odyssey was no regular cruise ship, though, and that makes the guests' predicament even bigger. It was a residential cruise ship, one that promised guests either 15+ years of living at sea full time or, conversely, the possibility to book extended, 3.5-year cruises. These cruises would be split into segments, so customers could buy segments, full cruises, or jump the shark and buy a villa to call home for the next 15 years.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Many of those now stranded in Cambodia either sold their houses and liquidated their businesses or spent all of their savings on the dream of having a home at sea, which is what VVR promised.
A five-year lease of a cabin started at $60,000, while a permanent cabin started at $120,000, but cruise prices were more affordable than with an established cruise liner. To these prices, residents also had to pay a monthly fee (between $3,300 and $9,500) for services like food, drinks, medical, WiFi, housekeeping, and assorted costs.
The official line In a statement to the media, VVR says that exorbitant fuel prices forced the decision, citing $1,800 monthly fuel costs per cabin at the beginning of the year that had ballooned to as much as $8,000, mostly due to the war in Iran. The company says that they've tried everything in their power to cut down costs and thus save fuel for months, including by reducing time spent at sea and spending more time in port.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences They mention that the high fuel costs couldn't and shouldn't fall on the guests, since they would be in no capacity to absorb them either way. This was no easy decision, but it is a necessary one , while the company tries to find financing elsewhere.
"Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured," VVR says.
Guests disembarked in Cambodia are being offered the proper support to find temporary living arrangements, the company continues. They don't go into specifics, but the general vibe is that they're paying for meals and lodging, which is exactly what they should be doing since those very people called the Odyssey their home by contract.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences The reality: 200+ people kicked out of their home, which happened to be on the ship The reality is… not what VVR would like the world to believe it is. Guests no longer bound by NDAs are taking to social media to offer their own version of events, speaking of poor management and poor planning since the start of the Odyssey, culminating in a heartless email in which they were informed they had less than six hours to gather all their belongings and disembark by 2 P.M.
They have not been offered accommodation, meals, a budget, or even as much as an apology or a proper explanation, Randy Cassingham on ResidentialCruising.com states . They were told to get off the ship and then left to their own devices, as if they were not legal owners of the cabins onboard but clandestine guests ferried illegally across the border.
VVR did reach out with some support, Cassingham says, but it was only after 72 hours after they were kicked off the ship – and then, too, with just a list of local hotels where they would have to pay for lodging themselves.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Guests are also challenging the official line about rising fuel prices being the main cause. Cassingham, for one, says there was "a cascade of problems" in the months prior to the decision, all of which pointed to poor management at the highest level.
A Ponzi scheme disguised as residential cruise ship? That's the unspoken message you get if you go down the rabbit hole on reddit, Facebook , or even YouTube. VVR has been acting shady from the start, even before the Odyssey set sail after months of delay, even "terminating" a couple of guests on claims of harboring a toxic, negative environment among the residents but in reality silencing them for daring to ask pertinent questions regarding the company's lack of transparency on almost everything.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Itineraries kept changing, the list of promised amenities changed completely by the time the Odyssey left the original port in Belfast, and there were constant reports about underwhelming conditions onboard, from faulty toilets to flooding, bad food, and cabins ("villas") that looked nothing like the renders with which they were advertised online.
It's true, the Odyssey was never marketed as a luxury residential cruise, but it was billed as "the world's first never-ending residential cruise" (*not true, that would be The World) that would allow you to comfortably live onboard while you traveled the world non-stop . But even by these standards, the old 1993 Fred. Olsen ship Braemar with a new lick of paint and newer furniture, was not prepared for the adventure laid out for it.
Odyssey set sail in October 2024, though the initial start date was set in May of that same year, and problems never seemed to stop. By April 2026, it was clear for many guests that the company was struggling: during a "town hall" meeting, they were asked to raise $3 million for an emergency loan .
Photo: Villa Vie Residences In September 2026, another urgent requests went off on the official communication channels, asking for $360,000 to pay for fuel, or the Odyssey risked being laid up indeterminately. This eventually turned out to be the case, even though some guests are saying that money WAS raised on both occasions.
Ironically, while this was happening, while VVR was having trouble with money, they were announcing expansion plans. Last summer, they announced a new line of high-end residential cruises called Avora Residences, with the flagship called Lumina to be next to launch to water.
Shortly after, they announced a sister ship for the Odyssey, Legacy , which would set sail in 2029. While guests were being disembarked off the Odyssey, VVR was still taking money for reservations on both these new and non-existent ships.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Current and former residents, as well as casual observers, speculate on the possibility of this being some sort of Ponzi scheme in residential cruise ship disguise. Most cabin owners and guests did not own a stake in the venture but some of the early adopters of this new ways of global living, who also happened to be "influencers" who PR-ed heavily for VVR and the Odyssey and brought in new clients, did. Some tapped out before this month's anti-climatic events.
The story is still unfolding, but even knowing this, the predicted outcome isn't rosy.
